text: It is 2:47 in the morning and you are still at your desk. You were supposed to be asleep three hours ago. Phone died at 1. Laptop open to a tab you stopped reading at 1:40. Only light in the room is the yellow desk lamp from the campus bookstore. That lamp is the reason you are still alive.
First thing you hear is not a scream. First thing you hear is your front door opening down the hall. Front door opens, front door closes. You live alone. You have lived alone eight months.

Somebody is walking down your hallway in shoes that are not your shoes. Slow. Not in a hurry. They walk like they know exactly where the kitchen is. You reach for your phone. Your hand closes on the charging cable where the phone is not. It is still dead on the nightstand.

The footsteps stop outside your bedroom door. They do not knock. They do not jiggle the handle. They just stand there. You can hear breathing on the other side. It is not the breathing of a person looking for your laptop. It is the breathing of a person who forgot how breathing works and is doing it from memory.
They walk away. Into the bathroom. Faucet runs fourteen seconds, stops. Toilet lid up, not down. They walk into the living room and they stop.
This is how it starts. Not with a siren. Not with a neighbor screaming. It starts with a stranger using your faucet at 2:49 in the morning.

You lock the door. It has a push-button that pops if you turn the handle hard enough. You push it anyway. The desk chair has wheels and is the worst doorstop in the world. You learn that. You swap it for the bookshelf. Dresser against the bookshelf. Mattress propped up against the dresser like the world's softest shield. You turn the lamp off. The room goes black. In the black you notice the three-quarter inch gap under the door. Through it you can see a wrong gray light.
At 3:14 the footsteps come back. They stop at the door. Through the gap: Mr. Henderson's sneakers. He pushes. Bookshelf does not move. He pushes harder. Mattress absorbs it. He walks away.
They do not hunt. They return. Mr. Henderson comes on a seventy-five minute cycle. 3:14, 4:32, 5:48, 7:03. Between visits he stands in your living room and breathes.
Second problem: the window. Second floor. The lock broke in April and you never fixed it. You wedge a ruler in the track. Close the blinds. Open them an inch.

Third problem: supplies. Half a water. Two granola bars. Twelve-pack of soda under the desk. Ibuprofen. A textbook. And your cat, under the bed the whole time. You move everything into the closet. The closet is the deepest place in the room.

At 8:18 there is tapping on the window. Three quiet taps, pause, two. The dead do not tap. It is the girl from 3B, the one who feeds your cat when you are out of town. She is alive. Hammer in her belt. One finger over her mouth. She passes you a bottle of water and four batteries through a three-inch gap. She says the living knock three times. She climbs to the roof.
The batteries fit a flashlight at the bottom of your backpack. You point it at the ceiling so the light bounces and does not reach the door.

At 9:47 there is a crash down the hall. A man kicks in a door. Drawers, fridge, a man's angry voice. Eleven minutes of silence. Then the scream. A crowd surges down the hall and that is the end of him. You understand it. The dead turn toward loud things the way moths turn toward light. You are alive because you have not made a sound in seven hours.

Fourth problem: your clock radio kicks on by itself at 11:00. Pop music, full volume, seven seconds before you rip the cord out. Seven seconds is enough. Something hits the bookshelf. The mattress holds. You sit in the closet with the cat in your lap and your hand over its mouth for thirty minutes while the crowd drifts away.

You build a weapon out of your twin-bell alarm clock. Tape it to a textbook. Tie extension cord to the book. Lower it out the window. Set for three. At three o'clock it rings. The bells are the loudest thing the street has heard. Every dead thing for two blocks turns and surges toward it, away from you. For the first time since 2:47 the other side of your door is silent.
Mr. Henderson comes back at 3:14, stands a while, walks away.
Twenty-five hours in. Inventory on the wall in ballpoint: Night 1. Henderson 75 min. Three knocks = friend. Loud = somewhere else. Cat: still here. Shift not over.
At 11:17 PM — tapping on the window. Three taps, pause, two. The girl is back. She has more water and cat food. She is going to the roof. Do you want to come.

You look at your door. The bookshelf, the dresser, the mattress, the note on the wall. The cat staring from under the bed. You look at the girl on the fire escape under the same moon. You pick up the cat. You put on the backpack. You turn the desk lamp ON so anything looking at the door still thinks you are in the chair. You climb out the window. The door stays closed. The lamp stays on. Night two starts on the roof.
